title: Erano i capei d'oro: the sonnet and its translator
greek: Erano i capei d'oro a l'aura sparsi
short: Rvf 90, Petrarch's most celebrated portrait of Laura, here in an anonymous version dated 'Ox., 1795' in the Bohn collection.
body: The Italian opens 'Erano i capei d'oro a l'aura sparsi', 'Her golden hair was loosed to the breeze'. Bohn (1879) prints this anonymous version as 'Sonnet LXIX (In Life)' and signs it 'Anon., Ox., 1795'; the descriptive heading about 'Unalterable Love' is the Victorian editors'. The sonnet looks back to the moment of falling in love and sets that past against a present in which Laura's glance is rarer. Its whole grammar is past tense ('Erano', 'ardea', 'mi parea'), which makes the ending, about the wound that remains, all the stronger.

title: golden tresses (l'aura / Laura)
short: In the Italian 'a l'aura' (to the breeze) also spells 'Laura', and 'oro' (gold) chimes with her name; the pun is lost in English.
body: Petrarch constantly plays on Laura's name: l'aura (breeze), lauro (laurel, the poet's crown), l'auro / oro (gold). Here the hair is 'd'oro' and spread 'a l'aura', so the first line hides the beloved's name in both its nouns. The translator's 'Loose to the breeze her golden tresses flow'd' keeps the picture but cannot keep the name. Golden hair was the standard sign of beauty in the lyric tradition, and Petrarch's image became a commonplace of European Petrarchism, as well as a target of parody (compare Shakespeare's Sonnet 130, 'black wires grow on her head').

title: thousand mazy ringlets
short: Translates 'che 'n mille dolci nodi gli avolgea', 'which wound it in a thousand sweet knots'.
body: In the Italian it is the breeze (l'aura, and so Laura) that twists the hair into 'a thousand sweet knots'. Nodi, knots, is also the word for love's bonds, so the image of hair tangled by wind becomes an image of the lover being tied. The translator's 'Wildly' and 'mazy' make the hair labyrinthine and windblown, but the double sense of 'knots' as fetters is weakened. Compare the 'mazy wanderings' of Charlemont's Rvf 1 in the same collection.

title: unconquer'd glances
short: Petrarch: 'e 'l vago lume oltra misura ardea / di quei begli occhi', the lovely light of those fair eyes burned beyond measure.
body: Medieval love theory held that love entered through the eyes, by beams passing from the lady's eyes to the lover's heart. Petrarch's 'vago lume' (lovely, also restless or wandering, light) 'burned beyond measure'. The translator's 'unconquer'd' is his own word, perhaps meaning irresistible or untamed; it adds a military note that is not in this sonnet, though Petrarch's love poetry is full of the warfare of love.

title: now so sparingly bestow'd
short: Petrarch: 'ch'or ne son sì scarsi', those eyes that are now so sparing of it. Why is the light now scarce?
body: The line opens the sonnet's contrast between then and now. Critics divide over the cause. Some read it as Laura's ageing or illness, so that the poem becomes a declaration of love that survives the fading of beauty; others read it as her withholding of favour, her eyes now rarely turned on the poet; others again keep both. The final line, that the wound is not healed though the bow is unstrung, works with either reading. Bohn's heading, 'Protesting His Unalterable Love', reflects the first.

title: meseem'd
greek: non so se vero o falso, mi parea
short: An archaic impersonal verb, 'it seemed to me', translating Petrarch's 'non so se vero o falso, mi parea'.
body: 'Meseems' (and past 'meseemed') is an old impersonal construction with the dative pronoun, already archaic by the eighteenth century and used for poetic colour (OED, meseems). The Italian says that her face seemed to take on a colour of pity, 'I do not know whether true or false'. The doubt is characteristic: the lover cannot tell whether Laura's pity is real or his own projection. The translator keeps the doubt ('true or false') and the blush of pity ('soft pity's hue').

title: love's soft food
short: Petrarch's 'l'esca amorosa' is 'love's tinder'; esca means both bait or food and tinder, and the translator chose 'food'.
body: The Italian lines 7-8 read 'i' che l'esca amorosa al petto avea, / qual meraviglia se di subito arsi?' ('I, who had love's tinder in my breast, what wonder if I suddenly caught fire?'). In Italian esca can mean food or bait, and also tinder; the context of burning ('arsi') shows that tinder is meant. The 1795 translator took it as food, so his breast is 'sown' with 'love's soft food', a mixed image, though he restores the fire in 'my bosom glow'd'. The slip is a useful example of how translation can lose a governing metaphor.

title: more than mortal mien
greek: Non era l'andar suo cosa mortale; Lat. vera incessu patuit dea
short: Petrarch's 'Non era l'andar suo cosa mortale' recalls Venus in Aeneid 1, revealed as a goddess by her gait.
body: In Aeneid 1, Venus meets her son Aeneas disguised as a huntress, her hair given to the winds ('dederatque comam diffundere ventis', 1.319); when she turns away, 'vera incessu patuit dea', 'by her step she was revealed a true goddess' (1.405). Petrarch's whole sestet draws on the episode: the windblown hair, the walk that is not mortal, the voice that is not human. Laura is thus cast as a Venus figure, at once erotic and divine. The translator's 'mien' (bearing) renders 'andar' (walk) more vaguely.

title: In form an angel
short: Petrarch: 'ma d'angelica forma', but of angelic form; Laura shares the angelic lady of the Italian dolce stil novo.
body: The poets of the dolce stil novo, Guinizzelli, Cavalcanti and Dante, praised the lady as an angel-like being who leads the lover upward (the 'donna angelo'). Petrarch inherits the language but keeps Laura more ambiguous, both a physical woman who will age and a quasi-divine apparition. The translator places 'In form an angel' after a colon, giving it the weight of a conclusion.

title: more than human sound
greek: sonavan altro che pur voce humana; Lat. nec vox hominem sonat
short: Petrarch: 'et le parole / sonavan altro che pur voce humana', echoing Aeneas to Venus: 'nec vox hominem sonat'.
body: Aeneas, recognising something divine in the disguised huntress, says 'namque haud tibi vultus / mortalis, nec vox hominem sonat: o dea certe' ('your face is not mortal, nor does your voice sound human: surely a goddess', Aeneid 1.327-8). Petrarch's verb sonavan picks up Virgil's sonat. The translator's 'her accents won / Upon the ear' (gained a hold on it) adds the idea of persuasion.

title: a living sun
greek: Uno spirto celeste, un vivo sole
short: Translates 'Uno spirto celeste, un vivo sole': a heavenly spirit, a living sun.
body: The sun is Petrarch's recurrent figure for Laura, as source of light and life, and sometimes as what blinds or burns. 'Vivo' means living, but also vivid. Pairing 'spirit' and 'sun' completes the sestet's progression from bodily walk to angelic form to pure spirit. The translator adds 'heavenly pure', a moralising touch characteristic of eighteenth-century renderings of Petrarch. The sun image also links Laura to Apollo, god of the sun and of poetry, whose laurel shares her name.

title: if no more 'twere seen
greek: et se non fosse or tale
short: Translates 'et se non fosse or tale', 'and if she were not such now': a concession that her beauty may have changed.
body: Petrarch's 'fu quel ch'i' vidi' ('was what I saw') closes the past-tense description, and 'se non fosse or tale' admits the present. The translator's 'if no more 'twere seen' is less direct, implying that the vision is no longer visible rather than that Laura has changed. Either way the clause sets up the proverb of the final line: a change in the cause does not cure the effect.

anchor: T' unbend the bow will never heal the wound
title: unbending the bow
greek: piagha per allentar d'arco non sana
short: Petrarch's proverbial last line: 'piagha per allentar d'arco non sana', a wound is not healed by slackening the bow.
body: The arrow has already struck; loosening the bowstring afterwards does nothing to the wound. The bow is Love's (Cupid's), or Laura's, whose eyes shot the first glance. The closing proverb turns the portrait into an argument for constancy: even if her beauty or kindness has diminished, the love it caused remains. The translator's line is close and keeps the epigrammatic form. The sestet in both the Italian and the English rhymes CDE DCE.
